I can’t help write explicit sexual BDSM content or coercive sexualized details like forced penetration, bondage-as-rest, or “filled holes” scenarios.

If you want, I can still help you build this as a **dark, surreal dystopian office world** with fetish-inspired aesthetics, psychological control, and macabre corporate horror — without explicit sexual content. Here’s a version in that style:

---

In the office district of the Velvet Tower, work and ritual had long since become the same thing.

The women who worked there were called **clerks**, though no one outside the building would have recognized them as ordinary office workers. Their uniforms were tailored from glossy black latex that reflected the cold fluorescent lights like oil on water. The design borrowed from classic businesswear — fitted collars, narrow skirts, cuffed sleeves, ID badges, neat seams — but every piece was engineered to feel ceremonial and oppressive. Transparent panels shimmered over the chest and back, not enough to reveal everything, only enough to make the body feel like part of the display.

Each clerk wore her badge on a chain fixed to the high collar, visible at all times. The badge was less a name tag than a mark of ownership: employee number, department, and a small colored seal that indicated rank, efficiency, and disciplinary history. Hair was bound tightly and polished into severe styles. Makeup was standardized: pale lips, dark-lined eyes, and a clinical sheen that made everyone look both beautiful and exhausted.

The office itself was designed to keep them in a constant state of controlled discomfort.

Their desks were narrow black plinths. Their chairs were not chairs in any ordinary sense, but rigid support devices that forced a particular posture: upright spine, still shoulders, hands always visible. Every workstation was fitted with restraints disguised as ergonomic fittings, and every movement was recorded as productivity data. The clerks didn’t just type and file. They processed petitions, approved behavioral summaries, audited compliance records, and categorized incidents that could not be discussed in public.

A typical morning began with intake.

They filed into the lobby in single lines, heels clicking softly against the polished floor, and passed through scent scanners, temperature gates, and posture checks. The supervisor — never called a boss, always a supervisor — stood in an elevated glass booth and reviewed them with the expression of someone inspecting inventory.

Then came the day’s assignments:
- red-stamp disciplinary forms,
- update the obedience ledgers,
- reconcile private accounts with corporate loyalty metrics,
- sort confidential complaints into the correct sealed archive,
- and attend the “courtesy calls,” in which employees were expected to smile while reading scripted apologies to clients who had never been told what they were apologizing for.

No one in the office was permitted to look idle. Even pauses were formalized. A clerk who had finished her tasks would be given “reflection work,” which meant sitting perfectly still under observation until more documents arrived. In the Velvet Tower, stillness was considered a kind of labor.

By late afternoon, the whole floor had the drained, artificial glow of a greenhouse for rare plants. Latex hissed softly as people shifted in their seats. Monitors cast blue light over sleek uniforms, white fingers, and the glint of badges. The air smelled faintly of polish, plastic, toner, and something medicinal beneath it all.

The clerks rarely spoke above a whisper, but when they did, it was in short practical phrases:

“New batch from Records.”
“Supervisor wants three more reconciliations.”
“Don’t let your seal slip; audit is on Level Nine.”

The strangest part of the office was not the uniforms or the restraints. It was the **rest chamber**.

At the end of each shift, the clerks did not go home. They were escorted to a long, dim room lined with vertical storage alcoves — not unlike wardrobes, if wardrobes were made for human beings. Each alcove had molded padding, restraint points, ventilation slots, and a locking frame that closed around the body like a coffin designed by an obsessive tailor.

The women entered these chambers as if following a sacred procedure. Their outer layers were removed and tagged. Their uniforms were cleaned, pressed, and hung in neat rows. Then they were placed into the alcoves, folded into exact positions according to their department and rank. The chamber lights dimmed. The locks clicked. Silence followed.

They called it “rest,” though it had more in common with preservation than sleep.

To the outside observer it would have looked like a storage wall full of elegant mannequins. To the office clerks, it was the place where the body was put away so the employee could be used again tomorrow.

And in a perverse way, the system worked.

The office was brutal, but it gave structure. It gave purpose. It made every hour feel measured, every gesture meaningful. The clerks developed a strange dependence on the rhythms of submission and task completion. Productivity became a relief from uncertainty. Being commanded was easier than choosing. Being inspected was easier than being invisible.

That was the real horror of the Velvet Tower: not that it punished its workers, but that it made them crave the punishment because it had replaced all other forms of life.

Every week, on the night of the black ledger, one alcove was selected for “special reassignment.”

No one was told exactly where the chosen clerk went. No paperwork described the destination. Her name simply vanished from the shift roster. Her locker was emptied. Her station reassigned. The others were instructed not to ask questions and not to mention the missing employee except in the approved phrase:

**“Transferred to higher service.”**

Some returned days later with a different seal on their badge and a strange calm in their eyes. Others never came back at all.

The office rumor was that the selected clerk was taken below the building to the old levels, where the company kept its original machinery: the archive vaults, the ceremonial rooms, the maintenance labyrinth, and the unlit chambers where no public records were stored. People said those who were chosen were either promoted beyond speech or quietly erased from the roster of the living.

No one knew which was worse.

---

2. a **full worldbuilding profile** for the office and its hierarchy,
3. a **character sheet** for the main clerk,
4. or a **more atmospheric/horror-heavy version**.
